1	# Output Modes
2	
3	Standout supports multiple output formats through a single handler because modern CLI tools serve two masters: human operators and machine automation.
4	
5	The same handler logic produces styled terminal output for eyes, plain text for logs, or structured JSON for `jq` pipelines—controlled entirely by the user's `--output` flag. This frees you from writing separate "API" and "CLI" logic.
6	
7	## The OutputMode Enum
8	
9	```rust
10	pub enum OutputMode {
11	    Auto,       // Auto-detect terminal capabilities
12	    Term,       // Always use ANSI escape codes
13	    Text,       // Never use ANSI codes (plain text)
14	    TermDebug,  // Keep style tags as [name]...[/name]
15	    Json,       // Serialize as JSON (skip template)
16	    Yaml,       // Serialize as YAML (skip template)
17	    Xml,        // Serialize as XML (skip template)
18	    Csv,        // Serialize as CSV (skip template)
19	}
20	```
21	
22	Three categories:
23	
24	**Templated modes** (Auto, Term, Text): Render the template, vary ANSI handling.
25	
26	**Debug mode** (TermDebug): Render the template, keep tags as literals for inspection.
27	
28	**Structured modes** (Json, Yaml, Xml, Csv): Skip the template entirely, serialize handler data directly.
29	
30	## Auto Mode
31	
32	`Auto` is the default. It queries the terminal for color support:
33	
34	```rust
35	Term::stdout().features().colors_supported()
36	```
37	
38	If colors are supported, Auto behaves like Term (ANSI codes applied). If not, Auto behaves like Text (tags stripped).
39	
40	This detection happens at render time, not startup. Piping output to a file or another process typically disables color support, so:
41	
42	```bash
43	myapp list              # Colors (if terminal supports)
44	myapp list > file.txt   # No colors (not a TTY)
45	myapp list | less       # No colors (pipe)
46	```
47	
48	## The --output Flag
49	
50	Standout adds a global `--output` flag accepting these values:
51	
52	```bash
53	myapp list --output=auto        # Default
54	myapp list --output=term        # Force ANSI codes
55	myapp list --output=text        # Force plain text
56	myapp list --output=term-debug  # Show style tags
57	myapp list --output=json        # JSON serialization
58	myapp list --output=yaml        # YAML serialization
59	myapp list --output=xml         # XML serialization
60	myapp list --output=csv         # CSV serialization
61	```
62	
63	The flag is global—it applies to all subcommands.
64	
65	## Term vs Text
66	
67	**Term**: turns every resolved style tag into ANSI escape codes, including
68	when the destination is a pipe rather than a terminal:
69	
70	```bash
71	myapp list --output=term > colored.txt
72	```
73	
74	Useful when you want to preserve colors for later display (e.g., `less -R`).
75	
76	A `term` request is unconditional, and the environment's color conventions do
77	not override it: `NO_COLOR=1 myapp list --output=term` still emits ANSI, the
78	same way `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 myapp list --output=text` still emits none. `auto`
79	is the only mode the environment reaches, and it reaches it through one value:
80	the destination's reported color capability. `auto` resolves to `term` when
81	that capability is reported and to `text` when it is not. `NO_COLOR` and
82	`TERM=dumb` suppress the capability, so they turn `auto` plain;
83	`CLICOLOR_FORCE` is not part of that capability probe, so it never turns `auto`
84	into `term`.
85	
86	**Text**: removes Standout's own style tags and adds no ANSI of its own:
87	
88	```bash
89	myapp list --output=text
90	```
91	
92	Useful for clean output regardless of terminal capabilities, or when processing output with other tools.
93	
94	Neither `term` nor `text` touches ANSI bytes that a handler or template
95	writes literally into the rendered text — the framework does not sanitize
96	those bytes and does not promise to. A caller that needs them gone strips
97	them itself.
98	
99	`term-debug` (which shows tags as `[name]...[/name]` rather than resolving
100	them) is internal: its tag vocabulary and exact spelling may change in any
101	release, so don't build automation against its output the way you might
102	against `term` or `text`.
103	
104	## TermDebug Mode
105	
106	TermDebug preserves style tags instead of converting them:
107	
108	```text
109	Template: [title]Hello[/title]
110	Output:   [title]Hello[/title]
111	```
112	
113	Use cases:
114	
115	- Debugging template issues
116	- Verifying style tag placement
117	- Automated testing of template output
118	
119	Unlike Term mode, unknown tags don't get the `?` marker in TermDebug.
120	TermDebug shows tag placement; it does not check whether a tag has a matching
121	style definition. Use `validate_template` when validation is required.
122	
123	## Structured Modes
124	
125	Structured modes bypass the template entirely. Handler data is serialized directly:
126	
127	```rust
128	#[derive(Serialize)]
129	struct ListOutput {
130	    items: Vec<Item>,
131	    total: usize,
132	}
133	
134	fn list_handler(...) -> HandlerResult<ListOutput> {
135	    Ok(Output::Render(ListOutput { items, total: items.len() }))
136	}
137	```
138	
139	```bash
140	myapp list --output=json
141	```
142	
143	```json
144	{
145	  "items": [...],

# Output Modes

Standout supports multiple output formats through a single handler because modern CLI tools serve two masters: human operators and machine automation.

The same handler logic produces styled terminal output for eyes, plain text for logs, or structured JSON for `jq` pipelines—controlled entirely by the user's `--output` flag. This frees you from writing separate "API" and "CLI" logic.

## The OutputMode Enum

```rust
pub enum OutputMode {
    Auto,       // Auto-detect terminal capabilities
    Term,       // Always use ANSI escape codes
    Text,       // Never use ANSI codes (plain text)
    TermDebug,  // Keep style tags as [name]...[/name]
    Json,       // Serialize as JSON (skip template)
    Yaml,       // Serialize as YAML (skip template)
    Xml,        // Serialize as XML (skip template)
    Csv,        // Serialize as CSV (skip template)
}
```

Three categories:

**Templated modes** (Auto, Term, Text): Render the template, vary ANSI handling.

**Debug mode** (TermDebug): Render the template, keep tags as literals for inspection.

**Structured modes** (Json, Yaml, Xml, Csv): Skip the template entirely, serialize handler data directly.

## Auto Mode

`Auto` is the default. It queries the terminal for color support:

```rust
Term::stdout().features().colors_supported()
```

If colors are supported, Auto behaves like Term (ANSI codes applied). If not, Auto behaves like Text (tags stripped).

This detection happens at render time, not startup. Piping output to a file or another process typically disables color support, so:

```bash
myapp list              # Colors (if terminal supports)
myapp list > file.txt   # No colors (not a TTY)
myapp list | less       # No colors (pipe)
```

## The --output Flag

Standout adds a global `--output` flag accepting these values:

```bash
myapp list --output=auto        # Default
myapp list --output=term        # Force ANSI codes
myapp list --output=text        # Force plain text
myapp list --output=term-debug  # Show style tags
myapp list --output=json        # JSON serialization
myapp list --output=yaml        # YAML serialization
myapp list --output=xml         # XML serialization
myapp list --output=csv         # CSV serialization
```

The flag is global—it applies to all subcommands.

## Term vs Text

**Term**: turns every resolved style tag into ANSI escape codes, including
when the destination is a pipe rather than a terminal:

```bash
myapp list --output=term > colored.txt
```

Useful when you want to preserve colors for later display (e.g., `less -R`).

A `term` request is unconditional, and the environment's color conventions do
not override it: `NO_COLOR=1 myapp list --output=term` still emits ANSI, the
same way `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 myapp list --output=text` still emits none. `auto`
is the only mode the environment reaches, and it reaches it through one value:
the destination's reported color capability. `auto` resolves to `term` when
that capability is reported and to `text` when it is not. `NO_COLOR` and
`TERM=dumb` suppress the capability, so they turn `auto` plain;
`CLICOLOR_FORCE` is not part of that capability probe, so it never turns `auto`
into `term`.

**Text**: removes Standout's own style tags and adds no ANSI of its own:

```bash
myapp list --output=text
```

Useful for clean output regardless of terminal capabilities, or when processing output with other tools.

Neither `term` nor `text` touches ANSI bytes that a handler or template
writes literally into the rendered text — the framework does not sanitize
those bytes and does not promise to. A caller that needs them gone strips
them itself.

`term-debug` (which shows tags as `[name]...[/name]` rather than resolving
them) is internal: its tag vocabulary and exact spelling may change in any
release, so don't build automation against its output the way you might
against `term` or `text`.

## TermDebug Mode

TermDebug preserves style tags instead of converting them:

```text
Template: [title]Hello[/title]
Output:   [title]Hello[/title]
```

Use cases:

- Debugging template issues
- Verifying style tag placement
- Automated testing of template output

Unlike Term mode, unknown tags don't get the `?` marker in TermDebug.
TermDebug shows tag placement; it does not check whether a tag has a matching
style definition. Use `validate_template` when validation is required.

## Structured Modes

Structured modes bypass the template entirely. Handler data is serialized directly:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ListOutput {
    items: Vec<Item>,
    total: usize,
}

fn list_handler(...) -> HandlerResult<ListOutput> {
    Ok(Output::Render(ListOutput { items, total: items.len() }))
}
```

```bash
myapp list --output=json
```

```json
{
  "items": [...],
  "total": 42
}
```

Same handler, same types—different output format. This enables:

- Machine-readable output for scripts
- Integration with other tools (`jq`, etc.)
- API-like behavior from CLI apps

### CSV Output

Normal `App` dispatch flattens the serializable handler data automatically for
CSV. That is the same handler data used by the other structured modes; handlers
should not inspect the requested mode or return a CSV-specific shape.

The standalone rendering API also supports direct `FlatDataSpec` rendering when
a caller needs explicit columns and headers:

```rust
use standout::tabular::{Column, FlatDataSpec, Width};
use standout::OutputMode;
use standout_render::render_auto_with_spec;

let spec = FlatDataSpec::builder()
    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("name").header("Name"))
    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("meta.role").header("Role"))
    .build();

render_auto_with_spec(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Csv, Some(&spec))?
```

The `key` field uses dot notation for nested paths (`"meta.role"` extracts `data["meta"]["role"]`).

When a command's canonical response is an object containing the CSV rows,
attach a presentation-layer projection through `CommandConfig`:

```rust
use serde_json::json;
use standout::cli::FnHandler;
use standout::tabular::{Column, Width};
use standout::{CsvProjection, StructuredOutputProjection};

let projection = StructuredOutputProjection::csv(
    CsvProjection::builder("items")
        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("language").header("LANGUAGE"))
        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("code").header("CODE"))
        .derived_column(
            Column::new(Width::default()).header("NET"),
            |row, _root| json!(
                row["code"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
                    - row["comments"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
            ),
        )
        .synthetic_row(|root| json!({
            "language": "TOTAL",
            "code": root["totals"]["code"],
            "comments": root["totals"]["comments"]
        }))
        .conditional_row(|root| {
            (root["skipped"].as_u64().unwrap_or(0) > 0)
                .then(|| json!({ "language": "SKIPPED" }))
        })
        .build(),
);

App::builder().command_with("summary", FnHandler::new(summary_handler), |config| {
    config.structured_output_projection(projection)
})?;
```

Direct-column dot paths are resolved against each selected row. Derived
columns receive both the current row and the root response. Synthetic-row
callbacks receive the root response and run in registration order. Column
ordering, headers, and `null_repr` use the existing `FlatDataSpec` behavior.

The projection applies only to CSV. Text and terminal modes still use the
template, while JSON, YAML, and XML serialize the canonical response. In the
pipeline, post-dispatch hooks run before projection and post-output hooks run
after it; `run`, `run_with`, output-file handling, and final emission
therefore all observe the same projected CSV.

See [Introduction to Tabular](../crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md) for
tabular specifications and layout.

## File Output

The `--output-file-path` flag redirects output to a file:

```bash
myapp list --output-file-path=results.txt
myapp list --output=json --output-file-path=data.json
```

Behavior:

- Text output: written to file, nothing printed to stdout
- Binary output: written to the requested file instead of stdout
- Silent output: no-op

After writing to file, stdout output is suppressed to prevent double-printing.

## Customizing Flags

Rename or disable the flags via `AppBuilder`:

```rust
App::builder()
    .output_flag(Some("format"))       // --format instead of --output
    .output_file_flag(Some("out"))     // --out instead of --output-file-path
    .build()?
```

```rust
App::builder()
    .no_output_flag()                  // Disable --output entirely
    .no_output_file_flag()             // Disable file output
    .build()?
```

## Keep Output Mode Out of Handlers

Output mode is a rendering concern and is deliberately absent from
`CommandContext`. A handler should return the same serializable data regardless
of whether the caller selected terminal, text, or structured output. If a
command's behavior genuinely differs, model that as an explicit command or
argument rather than an implicit presentation-mode branch.

## Rendering Without CLI

For standalone rendering with explicit mode:

```rust
use standout::{render_auto, OutputMode};

// Renders template for Term/Text, serializes for Json/Yaml
let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
```

The "auto" in `render_auto` refers to template-vs-serialize dispatch, not color detection.

For full control over both output mode and color mode:

```rust
use standout::{render_with_mode, ColorMode};

let output = render_with_mode(
    template,
    &data,
    &theme,
    OutputMode::Term,
    ColorMode::Dark,
)?;
```

# Error Handling

Standout owns the shell adapter: handlers and hooks return errors as data, and
`App::run` performs the final stderr write and process exit. Ordinary handler,
hook, render, pipe, and final-write failures use status `1`; Clap usage failures
use status `2`.

## Ordinary application errors

Return ordinary errors through `HandlerResult` with `?`. Standout formats the
message as `Error: {error}` — the error's own `Display` text after that fixed
prefix — reports it under `RunErrorKind::Handler`, and exits with status `1`:

```rust
fn handler(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<View> {
    let view = load_view()?;
    Ok(Output::Render(view))
}
```

A hook error is framed differently today: `Hook error: {error}` under
`RunErrorKind::Hook(phase)`. A handler failure and a hook failure therefore
read as two distinct diagnostics rather than one shared shape. Settling on a
single framing for both is tracked in issue #357, in the ROB06 adopter-seams
epic; until then, treat today's wording as an implementation detail rather
than something to match against in tests.

Do not print or call `process::exit` from handlers. This keeps capture APIs,
`TestHarness`, output ownership, and real process behavior on the same seam.

## Preserving an authoritative external failure

Use `ExternalFailure` only when another operation owns the status and diagnostic
contract, such as a delegated Git invocation. Construction rejects status `0`.
The diagnostic is a verbatim stderr payload: Standout adds no `Error:` prefix
and no trailing newline.

```rust
use standout::cli::{ExternalFailure, HandlerResult};

fn handler(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<View> {
    let output = run_git()?;
    if !output.status.success() {
        let status = output.status.code().and_then(|code| u8::try_from(code).ok()).unwrap_or(1);
        let diagnostic = String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stderr).into_owned();
        return Err(ExternalFailure::new(status, diagnostic)?.into());
    }
    Ok(Output::Render(to_view(output)))
}
```

A supported pre-dispatch check uses the same `ExternalFailure` interface:

```rust
Hooks::new().pre_dispatch(|_matches, _ctx| {
    let failure = ExternalFailure::new(128, "fatal: repository not found\n")
        .expect("128 is nonzero");
    Err(HookError::pre_dispatch_external(failure))
})
```

The escape hatch is not an error-mapping registry. Wrapping an ordinary error
does not change its status, and external declarations are not recognized from
post-dispatch or post-output hooks. Attach an underlying cause with
`ExternalFailure::with_source` when one exists.

Capture callers match `result.outcome()` / `into_outcome()` as
`DispatchResult::Error`, then inspect `RunErrorKind::External`,
`error.exit_status()`, and `error.as_str()`. See
[Execution Outcomes](./execution-outcomes.md) and [Testing](./testing.md).

1	# Execution Outcomes
2	
3	Standout carries shell semantics as typed data from argument parsing through
4	dispatch, rendering, hooks, output files, and final writes. Applications can let
5	`App::run` own output without losing the distinction between a usage error and a
6	runtime failure.
7	
8	## Status and streams
9	
10	| Outcome | Stream used by `run()` | Status |
11	| --- | --- | --- |
12	| Help or version | stdout | `0` |
13	| Successful rendered text or binary | stdout | `0` |
14	| `Output::Silent` | none | `0` |
15	| `--output-file-path` success | file only | `0` |
16	| Artifact written to a file | bytes to the file, report to stdout | `0` |
17	| Artifact written to stdout | bytes to stdout, report to stderr | `0` |
18	| Artifact with no selectable destination | stderr | `1` |
19	| Clap usage error | stderr | `2` |
20	| Handler, hook, render, pipe, or write failure | stderr | `1` |
21	| Application-declared external failure | stderr | exact declared nonzero status |
22	
23	Framework warning flushing happens after the primary output and does not replace
24	its status. Warnings cover non-fatal framework-owned setup, resource-loading,
25	and accepted-input diagnostics, including answer-sheet parse warnings that do
26	not reject a questionnaire submission. A final text or binary write failure does
27	replace a successful status with `1`, except that `BrokenPipe` while writing
28	final rendered command text to stdout is successful early consumer termination.
29	
30	## Capturing typed metadata
31	
32	`run_with` keeps output in-process and returns `CompletedRun`: the dispatch
33	outcome plus any framework warnings collected during the run. `Deref` keeps
34	string-oriented accessors and typed methods (`exit_status()`, `success_kind()`,
35	`error_kind()`) working on the wrapper. Pattern matching needs `outcome()` or
36	`into_outcome()`, because `CompletedRun` is not the variant enum.
37	
38	```rust
39	use standout::cli::{
40	    CompletedRun, DispatchResult, ExitStatus, OutputKind, RunError, RunErrorKind, SuccessKind,
41	};
42	use standout::{InputSources, TargetProperties};
43	
44	let result = app.run_with(
45	    command,
46	    args,
47	    TargetProperties::detect(),
48	    InputSources::from_process(),
49	);
50	let _ = result.warnings();
51	
52	match result.outcome() {
53	    DispatchResult::Handled(output) => println!("{}", output),
54	    DispatchResult::Binary(bytes, filename) => consume(bytes, filename),
55	    DispatchResult::Artifact(run) => {
56	        use std::io::{self, Write};
57	        if run.destination().is_stdout() {
58	            let mut stdout = io::stdout();
59	            stdout.write_all(run.bytes()).and_then(|()| stdout.flush()).map_err(|error| {
60	                RunError::new(
61	                    format!("Error writing artifact stdout: {}", error),
62	                    RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
63	                )
64	            })?;
65	            if let Some(report) = run.report().filter(|r| !r.is_empty()) {
66	                let mut stderr = io::stderr();
67	                writeln!(stderr, "{}", report).and_then(|()| stderr.flush()).map_err(|error| {
68	                    RunError::new(
69	                        format!("Error writing artifact report: {}", error),
70	                        RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
71	                    )
72	                })?;
73	            }
74	        } else if let Some(report) = run.report().filter(|r| !r.is_empty()) {
75	            let mut stdout = io::stdout();
76	            writeln!(stdout, "{}", report).and_then(|()| stdout.flush()).map_err(|error| {
77	                RunError::new(
78	                    format!("Error writing artifact report: {}", error),
79	                    RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
80	                )
81	            })?;
82	        }
83	    }
84	    DispatchResult::Error(error) => eprintln!("{}", error),
85	    DispatchResult::NoMatch(_matches) => {}
86	    DispatchResult::Silent => {}
87	    _ => {}
88	}
89	
90	assert_eq!(result.exit_status(), Some(ExitStatus::SUCCESS));
91	assert_eq!(result.success_kind(), Some(SuccessKind::Command));
92	assert_eq!(result.error_kind(), None);
93	```
94	
95	Use `into_outcome()` when the fallback needs owned `ArgMatches`
96	(`DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches)`).
97	
98	`RunOutput` and `RunError` dereference to `str`, implement `Display`, and expose
99	`as_str()` / `into_string()` for callers that used the tuple payloads as text.
100	`RunOutput::kind()` names a success the same way: `Command` for a handler's
101	output, `ClapHelp` / `ClapVersion` for a help or version display, and
102	`PagedHelp` for a `help --page` display — the text is identical, but the kind
103	tells a printing caller the user asked for a pager.
104	`RunError::kind()` identifies `ClapUsage`, `Handler`, `Hook(phase)`, `Render`, or
105	`FinalWrite(Text|Binary|Artifact)`. `External` identifies the narrow
106	application-declared external path; its `exit_status()` is the exact declared
107	nonzero status and its text is the verbatim diagnostic payload.
108	
109	## No-match is a handoff, not an error
110	
111	`DispatchResult::NoMatch` retains the parsed `ArgMatches` for partial adoption. It has
112	no framework exit status: `exit_status()` returns `None`, `run()` returns
113	`false`, and Standout emits nothing. The fallback dispatcher still owns that
114	command and its eventual status.
115	
116	The reverse direction never hands off. Before parsing, `run` and
117	`run_with` check every registered path against the clap `Command`: a
118	handler registered under a path the CLI declares no subcommand for is
119	unreachable — no invocation can name it and no fallback owns it, since the app
120	did register a handler. That returns `DispatchResult::Error` naming the
121	registered path, and the clap spelling too when the two differ only by `-`
122	versus `_` (`list_units` registered against a CLI declaring `list-units`).
123	`App::verify_command` reports the same mismatch at setup time.
124	
125	That check reads canonical command names only. Clap resolves an alias to the
126	command it names before `ArgMatches` reports it, so dispatch never sees the
127	alias: a handler registered as `ls` against `Command::new("list").alias("ls")`
128	is reached by neither spelling and is reported as unreachable. Registering
129	`list` is what makes both `list` and `ls` run the handler.
130	
131	## Framework-owned final writes
132	
133	`run()` writes successful text and binary bytes to stdout, diagnostics to
134	stderr, and exits with the typed non-zero status when execution fails. The one
135	exception is a paged help display (`SuccessKind::PagedHelp`), which goes to the
136	pager instead; if no pager is available it falls back to stdout, so help is
137	never lost. A closed
138	downstream pipe is not an error only for final rendered command text:
139	`BrokenPipe` there means the consumer stopped reading early. Binary stdout
140	writes and artifact report writes keep their typed final-write failures. The
141	suggested filename on binary output remains available to capture callers; use
142	`--output-file-path` when the framework should write either text or binary to a
143	file instead of stdout.
144	
145	Capture APIs do not perform the final stdout/stderr write, but file redirection
146	is part of dispatch and therefore reports typed `FinalWrite` failures directly.
147	External failures are never redirected to an output file: they remain stderr
148	diagnostics when `run()` performs the final write.
149	
150	Capture-mode runs drain framework warnings instead of rendering them. The raw
151	capture path stores the batch in `standout-render`'s warning collector, and
152	`standout-test::TestHarness` exposes the batch through `TestResult::warnings()`
153	so tests can assert warning content deterministically.
154	
155	## Compound artifacts
156	
157	`Output::Artifact` extends the framework-owned write to commands that also have
158	something to say about it. The application returns bytes, an optional suggested
159	destination, and an optional report; Standout selects the destination, writes,
160	and only then renders the report with a receipt naming where the bytes landed.
161	Ordering is the guarantee: a failed write produces `FinalWrite(Artifact)` and no
162	report at all, so a success message can never promise a file that never
163	appeared.
164	
165	See [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for the
166	destination policy, the report envelope, and the artifact-to-stdout report
167	channel.

# Execution Outcomes

Standout carries shell semantics as typed data from argument parsing through
dispatch, rendering, hooks, output files, and final writes. Applications can let
`App::run` own output without losing the distinction between a usage error and a
runtime failure.

## Status and streams

| Outcome | Stream used by `run()` | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Help or version | stdout | `0` |
| Successful rendered text or binary | stdout | `0` |
| `Output::Silent` | none | `0` |
| `--output-file-path` success | file only | `0` |
| Artifact written to a file | bytes to the file, report to stdout | `0` |
| Artifact written to stdout | bytes to stdout, report to stderr | `0` |
| Artifact with no selectable destination | stderr | `1` |
| Clap usage error | stderr | `2` |
| Handler, hook, render, pipe, or write failure | stderr | `1` |
| Application-declared external failure | stderr | exact declared nonzero status |

Framework warning flushing happens after the primary output and does not replace
its status. Warnings cover non-fatal framework-owned setup, resource-loading,
and accepted-input diagnostics, including answer-sheet parse warnings that do
not reject a questionnaire submission. A final text or binary write failure does
replace a successful status with `1`, except that `BrokenPipe` while writing
final rendered command text to stdout is successful early consumer termination.

## Capturing typed metadata

`run_with` keeps output in-process and returns `CompletedRun`: the dispatch
outcome plus any framework warnings collected during the run. `Deref` keeps
string-oriented accessors and typed methods (`exit_status()`, `success_kind()`,
`error_kind()`) working on the wrapper. Pattern matching needs `outcome()` or
`into_outcome()`, because `CompletedRun` is not the variant enum.

```rust
use standout::cli::{
    CompletedRun, DispatchResult, ExitStatus, OutputKind, RunError, RunErrorKind, SuccessKind,
};
use standout::{InputSources, TargetProperties};

let result = app.run_with(
    command,
    args,
    TargetProperties::detect(),
    InputSources::from_process(),
);
let _ = result.warnings();

match result.outcome() {
    DispatchResult::Handled(output) => println!("{}", output),
    DispatchResult::Binary(bytes, filename) => consume(bytes, filename),
    DispatchResult::Artifact(run) => {
        use std::io::{self, Write};
        if run.destination().is_stdout() {
            let mut stdout = io::stdout();
            stdout.write_all(run.bytes()).and_then(|()| stdout.flush()).map_err(|error| {
                RunError::new(
                    format!("Error writing artifact stdout: {}", error),
                    RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
                )
            })?;
            if let Some(report) = run.report().filter(|r| !r.is_empty()) {
                let mut stderr = io::stderr();
                writeln!(stderr, "{}", report).and_then(|()| stderr.flush()).map_err(|error| {
                    RunError::new(
                        format!("Error writing artifact report: {}", error),
                        RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
                    )
                })?;
            }
        } else if let Some(report) = run.report().filter(|r| !r.is_empty()) {
            let mut stdout = io::stdout();
            writeln!(stdout, "{}", report).and_then(|()| stdout.flush()).map_err(|error| {
                RunError::new(
                    format!("Error writing artifact report: {}", error),
                    RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
                )
            })?;
        }
    }
    DispatchResult::Error(error) => eprintln!("{}", error),
    DispatchResult::NoMatch(_matches) => {}
    DispatchResult::Silent => {}
    _ => {}
}

assert_eq!(result.exit_status(), Some(ExitStatus::SUCCESS));
assert_eq!(result.success_kind(), Some(SuccessKind::Command));
assert_eq!(result.error_kind(), None);
```

Use `into_outcome()` when the fallback needs owned `ArgMatches`
(`DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches)`).

`RunOutput` and `RunError` dereference to `str`, implement `Display`, and expose
`as_str()` / `into_string()` for callers that used the tuple payloads as text.
`RunOutput::kind()` names a success the same way: `Command` for a handler's
output, `ClapHelp` / `ClapVersion` for a help or version display, and
`PagedHelp` for a `help --page` display — the text is identical, but the kind
tells a printing caller the user asked for a pager.
`RunError::kind()` identifies `ClapUsage`, `Handler`, `Hook(phase)`, `Render`, or
`FinalWrite(Text|Binary|Artifact)`. `External` identifies the narrow
application-declared external path; its `exit_status()` is the exact declared
nonzero status and its text is the verbatim diagnostic payload.

## No-match is a handoff, not an error

`DispatchResult::NoMatch` retains the parsed `ArgMatches` for partial adoption. It has
no framework exit status: `exit_status()` returns `None`, `run()` returns
`false`, and Standout emits nothing. The fallback dispatcher still owns that
command and its eventual status.

The reverse direction never hands off. Before parsing, `run` and
`run_with` check every registered path against the clap `Command`: a
handler registered under a path the CLI declares no subcommand for is
unreachable — no invocation can name it and no fallback owns it, since the app
did register a handler. That returns `DispatchResult::Error` naming the
registered path, and the clap spelling too when the two differ only by `-`
versus `_` (`list_units` registered against a CLI declaring `list-units`).
`App::verify_command` reports the same mismatch at setup time.

That check reads canonical command names only. Clap resolves an alias to the
command it names before `ArgMatches` reports it, so dispatch never sees the
alias: a handler registered as `ls` against `Command::new("list").alias("ls")`
is reached by neither spelling and is reported as unreachable. Registering
`list` is what makes both `list` and `ls` run the handler.

## Framework-owned final writes

`run()` writes successful text and binary bytes to stdout, diagnostics to
stderr, and exits with the typed non-zero status when execution fails. The one
exception is a paged help display (`SuccessKind::PagedHelp`), which goes to the
pager instead; if no pager is available it falls back to stdout, so help is
never lost. A closed
downstream pipe is not an error only for final rendered command text:
`BrokenPipe` there means the consumer stopped reading early. Binary stdout
writes and artifact report writes keep their typed final-write failures. The
suggested filename on binary output remains available to capture callers; use
`--output-file-path` when the framework should write either text or binary to a
file instead of stdout.

Capture APIs do not perform the final stdout/stderr write, but file redirection
is part of dispatch and therefore reports typed `FinalWrite` failures directly.
External failures are never redirected to an output file: they remain stderr
diagnostics when `run()` performs the final write.

Capture-mode runs drain framework warnings instead of rendering them. The raw
capture path stores the batch in `standout-render`'s warning collector, and
`standout-test::TestHarness` exposes the batch through `TestResult::warnings()`
so tests can assert warning content deterministically.

## Compound artifacts

`Output::Artifact` extends the framework-owned write to commands that also have
something to say about it. The application returns bytes, an optional suggested
destination, and an optional report; Standout selects the destination, writes,
and only then renders the report with a receipt naming where the bytes landed.
Ordering is the guarantee: a failed write produces `FinalWrite(Artifact)` and no
report at all, so a success message can never promise a file that never
appeared.

See [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for the
destination policy, the report envelope, and the artifact-to-stdout report
channel.

1	# Minimal single-crate example
2	
3	This self-contained project is a compact way to see Standout's dispatch and
4	rendering pipeline. It keeps everything in one binary package for brevity; it
5	is not the recommended layout for an application with reusable logic.
6	
7	For production-shaped ownership, continue to the
8	[two-package worked application](production-shaped-example.md), where a
9	CLI-free library owns application behavior and a binary owns all CLI concerns.
10	
11	## File structure
12	
13	```text
14	my-todo/
15	├── Cargo.toml
16	└── src/
17	    ├── main.rs
18	    ├── templates/list.jinja
19	    └── styles/default.css
20	```
21	
22	## Cargo.toml
23	
24	```toml
25	[package]
26	name = "my-todo"
27	version = "0.1.0"
28	edition = "2021"
29	
30	[dependencies]
31	standout = "9"
32	clap = { version = "4", features = ["derive"] }
33	serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
34	anyhow = "1"
35	```
36	
37	## `src/main.rs`
38	
39	```rust
40	use clap::{CommandFactory, Parser, Subcommand};
41	use serde::Serialize;
42	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
43	use standout::{embed_styles, embed_templates, handler};
44	
45	#[derive(Parser)]
46	#[command(name = "my-todo")]
47	struct Cli {
48	    #[command(subcommand)]
49	    command: Option<Commands>,
50	}
51	
52	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
53	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
54	enum Commands {
55	    /// List all todos. Running the binary with no command lists too.
56	    #[dispatch(pure, default)]
57	    List,
58	}
59	
60	#[derive(Serialize)]
61	struct TodoResult {
62	    todos: Vec<TodoView>,
63	}
64	
65	#[derive(Serialize)]
66	struct TodoView {
67	    title: String,
68	    status: String,
69	}
70	
71	mod handlers {
72	    use super::*;
73	
74	    // This is a CLI adapter returning view data. In a real application it
75	    // should call a CLI-free library rather than contain application behavior.
76	    #[handler]
77	    pub fn list(
78	        #[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext,
79	    ) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
80	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult {
81	            todos: vec![
82	                TodoView { title: "Write documentation".into(), status: "done".into() },
83	                TodoView { title: "Ship v1.0".into(), status: "pending".into() },
84	            ],
85	        }))
86	    }
87	}
88	
89	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
90	    let app = App::builder()
91	        .version(env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))
92	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
93	        .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
94	        .default_theme("default")
95	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
96	        .build()?;
97	
98	    app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
99	    Ok(())
100	}
101	```
102	
103	## `src/templates/list.jinja`
104	
105	```jinja
106	[title]My Todos[/title]
107	{% for todo in todos %}
108	[index]{{ loop.index }}.[/index] [{{ todo.status }}]{{ todo.title }}[/{{ todo.status }}]
109	{% endfor %}
110	```
111	
112	## `src/styles/default.css`
113	
114	```css
115	.title { color: cyan; font-weight: bold; }
116	.index { color: yellow; }
117	.done { color: gray; text-decoration: line-through; }
118	.pending { color: white; font-weight: bold; }
119	
120	@media (prefers-color-scheme: light) {
121	    .pending { color: black; }
122	}
123	```
124	
125	## Run it
126	
127	```bash
128	cargo run
129	cargo run -- list
130	cargo run -- list --output json
131	cargo run -- list --output text
132	```
133	
134	This demonstrates command dispatch, template rendering, structured output, hot
135	reload in debug builds, adaptive styles, and standout's themed `--help`, which
136	is on unless an application calls `.help_handling(false)`. It intentionally
137	does not teach package ownership or the testing pyramid; the
138	[production-shaped example](production-shaped-example.md) does.
139

1	# The Handler Contract
2	
3	Handlers are shell adapters: they map parsed CLI input to application calls and
4	return serializable CLI-owned view data. Keep reusable behavior in a CLI-free
5	library. The handler contract is designed to be **explicit** rather than
6	permissive, so adapters remain testable and decoupled from output formatting.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## Quick Start: The `#[handler]` Macro
11	
12	For most handlers, use the `#[handler]` macro to write typed adapter functions:
13	
14	```rust,ignore
15	use standout_macros::handler;
16	
17	#[handler]
18	pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool, #[arg] limit: Option<usize>) -> Result<Vec<Item>, anyhow::Error> {
19	    storage::list(all, limit)
20	}
21	```
22	
23	The macro leaves `list` alone and adds three items beside it:
24	
25	| Item | What it is |
26	| --- | --- |
27	| `list__handler(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext)` | reads the arguments out of `ArgMatches` and calls `list`. It returns **the annotated return type verbatim** — here `Result<Vec<Item>, anyhow::Error>`, not `HandlerResult<Vec<Item>>` |
28	| `list__expected_args() -> Vec<ExpectedArg>` | what `App::verify_command` reads |
29	| `list_Handler` | a unit struct implementing [`Handler`](#the-handler-trait) — **the registrable item** |
30	
31	The `Result<T, E>` to `Output::Render` wrap happens inside `list_Handler`'s
32	`Handler::handle`, which calls `IntoHandlerResult::into_handler_result` on
33	whatever `list__handler` returned. It is not applied by `list__handler` itself.
34	Only registration of `list_Handler` runs that wrap. `#[derive(Dispatch)]` does
35	not reach the trait object at all: it registers the closure
36	`handlers::list__handler` through `GroupBuilder::command_with`, so nothing
37	calls `Handler::handle` and the annotated return type has to be a
38	`HandlerResult` shape already. That is the difference the next two tables
39	spell out.
40	
41	The un-suffixed `handlers::list` is not registrable — it has the wrong
42	signature by design, so that a test can call it directly. Which of the other
43	two items you register depends on the method:
44	
45	| Method | What it takes | What to pass |
46	| --- | --- | --- |
47	| `AppBuilder::command_with` | `impl Handler` | `handlers::list_Handler` |
48	| `GroupBuilder::command` / `command_with`, and therefore `#[derive(Dispatch)]` | a closure returning `HandlerResult<T>` | `handlers::list__handler` |
49	
50	That second row constrains the return type, and it is the one place the two
51	registration paths genuinely differ. `list__handler` returns the annotated type
52	verbatim, so it satisfies `HandlerResult<T>` only when the function was written
53	`-> Result<Output<T>, E>` (or `-> Result<(), E>`, whose wrapper returns
54	`HandlerResult<()>`). **A handler annotated `-> Result<T, E>` cannot be
55	registered through `#[derive(Dispatch)]`**: expansion fails with `expected
56	list__handler to return Result<Output<_>, Error>, but it returns Result<Items,
57	Error>`. Write it `-> Result<Output<T>, E>`, or register `list_Handler` through
58	`AppBuilder::command_with`, where `Handler::handle` applies the wrap for you.
59	
60	The three return shapes, and the original functions still being callable:
61	
62	```rust
63	use standout::cli::{CommandContext, Output};
64	use standout::handler;
65	
66	#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
67	pub struct Items {
68	    pub names: Vec<String>,
69	}
70	
71	/// `Handler::Output` is `Items`; `handle` wraps the value in `Output::Render`.
72	#[handler]
73	pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Items, anyhow::Error> {
74	    let mut names = vec!["ssh".to_string()];
75	    if all {
76	        names.push("cron".to_string());
77	    }
78	    Ok(Items { names })
79	}
80	
81	/// `Handler::Output` is `Items`; the `Output` passes through untouched.
82	#[handler]
83	pub fn about(#[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<Items>, anyhow::Error> {
84	    Ok(Output::Render(Items { names: vec!["unitctl".to_string()] }))
85	}
86	
87	/// `Handler::Output` is `()`; `handle` produces `Output::Silent`.
88	#[handler]
89	pub fn reload(#[flag] _force: bool) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
90	    Ok(())
91	}
92	
93	fn main() {
94	    // No ArgMatches, no dispatcher: the annotated function is what a unit test calls.
95	    assert_eq!(list(true).unwrap().names, ["ssh", "cron"]);
96	    reload(false).unwrap();
97	}
98	```
99	
100	Every `#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` attribute is listed in the
101	[`#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` reference](../../../topics/dispatch-attributes.md).
102	
103	**Parameter Annotations:**
104	
105	| Annotation            | Type              | Extraction                    |
106	| --------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------- |
107	| `#[flag]`             | `bool`            | `matches.get_flag("name")`    |
108	| `#[flag(name = "x")]` | `bool`            | `matches.get_flag("x")`       |
109	| `#[arg]`              | `T`               | Required argument             |
110	| `#[arg]`              | `Option<T>`       | Optional argument             |
111	| `#[arg]`              | `Vec<T>`          | Multiple values               |
112	| `#[arg(name = "x")]`  | `T`               | Argument with custom CLI name |
113	| `#[ctx]`              | `&CommandContext` | Access to context             |
114	| `#[matches]`          | `&ArgMatches`     | Raw matches (escape hatch)    |
115	
116	Without `name = "x"`, the argument id is the parameter name with underscores
117	turned into hyphens: `no_legend` reads the argument id `no-legend`. Clap's own
118	derive ids an argument by the field name it comes from, so a clap-derive
119	`no_legend` field declares `#[arg(id = "no-legend")]` to meet the handler, or
120	the handler parameter takes the field's id with `#[flag(name = "no_legend")]`.
121	`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports the mismatch instead of leaving it to a
122	runtime `get_flag` panic. A parameter named with a raw identifier drops the
123	`r#` first, the way clap's derive drops it from a field name: `r#type` reads
124	the argument id `type`.
125	
126	**Return Type Handling:** the function must return `Result<T, E>`; the macro
127	rejects anything else with `handler must return Result<T, E>`. What `T` is
128	decides what `Handler::Output` becomes and whether anything is wrapped.
129	
130	| Annotated return type | `Handler::Output` | What `handle` produces |
131	| --- | --- | --- |
132	| `Result<T, E>` | `T` | `Ok(value)` wrapped in `Output::Render(value)` |
133	| `Result<Output<T>, E>` (that is, `HandlerResult<T>`) | `T` | the `Output` you returned, unchanged |
134	| `Result<(), E>` | `()` | `Output::Silent` |
135	
136	> **Testing:** The original function is preserved, so you can test directly: `list(true, Some(10))`.
137	
138	---
139	
140	## The Handler Trait
141	
142	```rust,ignore
143	pub trait Handler {
144	    type Output: Serialize;
145	    fn handle(&mut self, matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Self::Output>;
146	}
147	```
148	
149	Key characteristics:
150	
151	- **Mutable self**: `&mut self` allows direct state modification
152	- **Output must be Serialize**: Needed for JSON/YAML modes and template context
153	
154	Implementing the trait directly is useful when your handler needs internal state—database connections, configuration, caches, etc.
155	
156	### Example: Struct Handler with State
157	
158	```rust,ignore
159	use standout_dispatch::{Handler, Output, CommandContext, HandlerResult};
160	use clap::ArgMatches;
161	use serde::Serialize;
162	
163	struct CachingDatabase {
164	    connection: Connection,
165	    cache: HashMap<String, Vec<Row>>,
166	}
167	
168	impl CachingDatabase {
169	    fn query_with_cache(&mut self, sql: &str) -> Result<Vec<Row>, Error> {
170	        if let Some(cached) = self.cache.get(sql) {
171	            return Ok(cached.clone());
172	        }
173	        let result = self.connection.execute(sql)?;
174	        self.cache.insert(sql.to_string(), result.clone());
175	        Ok(result)
176	    }
177	}
178	
179	impl Handler for CachingDatabase {
180	    type Output = Vec<Row>;
181	
182	    fn handle(&mut self, matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Row>> {
183	        let query: &String = matches.get_one("query").unwrap();
184	        let rows = self.query_with_cache(query)?;  // &mut self works!
185	        Ok(Output::Render(rows))
186	    }
187	}
188	```
189	
190	---
191	
192	## Closure Handlers
193	
194	Most handlers are simple closures using `FnHandler`:
195	
196	```rust,ignore
197	use standout_dispatch::{FnHandler, Output, HandlerResult};
198	
199	let mut counter = 0;
200	
201	let handler = FnHandler::new(move |_matches, _ctx| {
202	    counter += 1;  // Mutation works!
203	    Ok(Output::Render(counter))
204	});
205	```
206	
207	The closure signature:
208	
209	```rust,ignore
210	fn(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T>
211	where T: Serialize
212	```
213	
214	Closures are `FnMut`, allowing captured variables to be mutated.
215	
216	---
217	
218	## SimpleFnHandler (No Context Needed)
219	
220	When your handler doesn't need `CommandContext`, use `SimpleFnHandler` for a cleaner signature:
221	
222	```rust,ignore
223	use standout_dispatch::SimpleFnHandler;
224	
225	let handler = SimpleFnHandler::new(|matches| {
226	    let verbose = matches.get_flag("verbose");
227	    let items = storage::list()?;
228	    Ok(ListResult { items, verbose })
229	});
230	```
231	
232	The closure signature:
233	
234	```rust,ignore
235	fn(&ArgMatches) -> Result<T, E>
236	where T: Serialize, E: Into<anyhow::Error>
237	```
238	
239	`SimpleFnHandler` automatically wraps the result in `Output::Render` via `IntoHandlerResult`.
240	
241	---
242	
243	## IntoHandlerResult Trait
244	
245	The `IntoHandlerResult` trait enables handlers to return `Result<T, E>` directly instead of `HandlerResult<T>`:
246	
247	```rust,ignore
248	use standout_dispatch::IntoHandlerResult;
249	
250	// Before: explicit Output wrapping
251	fn list(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
252	    let items = storage::list()?;
253	    Ok(Output::Render(items))
254	}
255	
256	// After: automatic conversion
257	fn list(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> impl IntoHandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
258	    storage::list()  // Result<Vec<Item>, Error> auto-converts
259	}
260	```
261	
262	The trait is implemented for:
263	
264	- `Result<T, E>` where `E: Into<anyhow::Error>` → wraps `Ok(t)` in `Output::Render(t)`
265	- `HandlerResult<T>` → passes through unchanged
266	
267	This is used internally by `SimpleFnHandler` and the `#[handler]` macro.
268	
269	---
270	
271	## HandlerResult
272	
273	`HandlerResult<T>` is a standard `Result` type:
274	
275	```rust,ignore
276	pub type HandlerResult<T> = Result<Output<T>, anyhow::Error>;
277	```
278	
279	The `?` operator works naturally for error propagation:
280	
281	```rust,ignore
282	fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Items> {
283	    let items = storage::load()?;           // Propagates errors
284	    let filtered = filter_items(&items)?;   // Propagates errors
285	    Ok(Output::Render(Items { filtered }))
286	}
287	```
288	
289	### Authoritative external failures
290	
291	When a handler delegates to another executable and the application's contract
292	requires that executable's exact nonzero status and stderr, return the public
293	`ExternalFailure` type through the same `HandlerResult` seam:
294	
295	```rust,ignore
296	let failure = ExternalFailure::new(128, git_stderr)?;
297	Err(failure.into())
298	```
299	
300	Construction rejects status `0`. Standout recognizes only this concrete type,
301	preserves its diagnostic verbatim, and exposes it as `RunErrorKind::External`.
302	Ordinary handler errors still use status `1`; this is not a general exit-code
303	mapping mechanism. Handlers must not print or call `process::exit` themselves.
304	
305	---
306	
307	## The Output Enum
308	
309	`Output<T>` represents what a handler produces:
310	
311	```rust,ignore
312	#[non_exhaustive]
313	pub enum Output<T: Serialize> {
314	    Render(T),
315	    Silent,
316	    Binary { data: Vec<u8>, filename: String },
317	    Artifact(Artifact<T>),
318	}
319	```
320	
321	`Output` is `#[non_exhaustive]`: matches on it need a `_` arm so later shapes
322	can be added without breaking downstream code.
323	
324	### Output::Render(T)
325	
326	The common case. Data is passed to the render function:
327	
328	```rust,ignore
329	#[derive(Serialize)]
330	struct ListResult {
331	    items: Vec<Item>,
332	    total: usize,
333	}
334	
335	fn list_handler(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ListResult> {
336	    let items = storage::list()?;
337	    Ok(Output::Render(ListResult {
338	        total: items.len(),
339	        items,
340	    }))
341	}
342	```
343	
344	### Output::Silent
345	
346	No output produced. Useful for commands with side effects only:
347	
348	```rust,ignore
349	fn delete_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<()> {
350	    let id: &String = matches.get_one("id").unwrap();
351	    storage::delete(id)?;
352	    Ok(Output::Silent)
353	}
354	```
355	
356	Silent behavior:
357	
358	- Post-output hooks still receive `RenderedOutput::Silent`
359	- Render function is not called
360	- Nothing prints to stdout
361	
362	### Output::Binary
363	
364	Raw bytes for file output:
365	
366	```rust,ignore
367	fn export_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<()> {
368	    let data = generate_report()?;
369	    let pdf_bytes = render_to_pdf(&data)?;
370	
371	    Ok(Output::Binary {
372	        data: pdf_bytes,
373	        filename: "report.pdf".into(),
374	    })
375	}
376	```
377	
378	Binary output bypasses the render function entirely.
379	
380	The filename is a **hint for the caller**, not permission to write. Without
381	`--output-file-path`, `run()` sends the bytes to stdout and touches no file. If
382	you want the framework to write the suggested destination, use `Output::Artifact`
383	— that opt-in is the whole difference between the two shapes.
384	
385	### Output::Artifact
386	
387	Owned bytes plus an application-owned report, for commands that produce a file
388	*and* have something to say about it. `Output::Binary` cannot carry a report,
389	and nothing renders after its write, so a command that wants to say "exported 12
390	rows to /tmp/report.csv (2 warnings)" would otherwise have to write the file
391	itself — pulling destination policy back into the application core.
392	
393	```rust,ignore
394	use standout::cli::{Artifact, HandlerResult, Output};
395	
396	#[derive(Serialize)]
397	struct ExportReport {
398	    exported: usize,
399	    warnings: Vec<Warning>,
400	}
401	
402	fn export_handler(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ExportReport> {
403	    let export = core::export_csv()?;   // bytes + facts, no filesystem
404	
405	    Ok(Output::Artifact(
406	        Artifact::new(export.csv)
407	            .suggest_destination(export.suggested_filename)
408	            .with_report(ExportReport {
409	                exported: export.rows,
410	                warnings: export.warnings,
411	            }),
412	    ))
413	}
414	```
415	
416	Who owns what:
417	
418	| Concern | Owner |
419	| --- | --- |
420	| Artifact bytes | Application |
421	| Suggested destination | Application (a suggestion) |
422	| Semantic report and warning taxonomy | Application |
423	| Destination selection | Framework |
424	| The write and its failure | Framework |
425	| Receipt (completed destination) | Framework |
426	
427	#### Destination policy
428	
429	Standout selects the destination deterministically:
430	
431	1. the explicit `--output-file-path` override;
432	2. the artifact's `suggest_destination(...)`, if the application opted in;
433	3. stdout, if the application opted in with `allow_stdout()`.
434	
435	If none applies, the run fails with `FinalWrite(Artifact)` rather than inventing
436	a file or dropping the bytes. All three steps share that one failure path.
437	
438	#### Write first, report second
439	
440	Standout writes, then renders the report from a fixed envelope:
441	
442	```json
443	{
444	  "report": { "exported": 12, "warnings": [] },
445	  "receipt": { "destination": "/tmp/report.csv", "stdout": false, "byte_count": 480 }
446	}
447	```
448	
449	So a template can say what only the framework knows:
450	
451	```jinja
452	Exported {{ report.exported }} rows to {{ receipt.destination }}
453	```
454	
455	The envelope shape is fixed (`report` + `receipt`) whatever the report's type,
456	so no application key can collide with the receipt. Structured modes serialize
457	the same envelope. A failed write renders nothing: success cannot outrun the
458	write that justifies it.
459	
460	#### The report channel
461	
462	Mixing a report into the bytes would corrupt them, so the channel follows the
463	destination:
464	
465	| Artifact destination | Report goes to |
466	| --- | --- |
467	| File | stdout |
468	| Stdout (`allow_stdout()`) | stderr |
469	
470	#### Hooks and artifacts
471	
472	Post-dispatch hooks see the report as ordinary handler data. Post-output hooks
473	see `RenderedOutput::Artifact` and can still transform the bytes or the report
474	via `as_artifact_mut()`. Hooks never perform the write — that stays framework-
475	owned, which is what keeps the failure path single and the report honest.
476	
477	Bytes are owned; streaming is deliberately not part of this contract.
478	
479	---
480	
481	## CommandContext
482	
483	`CommandContext` provides execution environment information and state access:
484	
485	```rust,ignore
486	pub struct CommandContext {
487	    pub command_path: Vec<String>,
488	    pub app_state: Rc<Extensions>,
489	    pub extensions: Extensions,
490	}
491	```
492	
493	**command_path**: The subcommand chain as a vector, e.g., `["db", "migrate"]`. Useful for logging or conditional logic.
494	
495	**app_state**: Shared, immutable state configured at app build time via `AppBuilder::app_state()`. Wrapped in `Arc` for cheap cloning. Use for database connections, configuration, API clients.
496	
497	**extensions**: Per-request, mutable state injected by pre-dispatch hooks. Use for user sessions, request IDs, computed values.
498	
499	> For comprehensive coverage of state management, see [App State and Extensions](app-state.md).
500	
501	---
502	
503	## State Access: App State vs Extensions
504	
505	Handlers access state through two distinct mechanisms with different semantics:
506	
507	| Aspect         | `ctx.app_state`               | `ctx.extensions`           |
508	| -------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------------- |
509	| **Mutability** | Immutable (`&`)               | Mutable (`&mut`)           |
510	| **Lifetime**   | App lifetime                  | Per-request                |
511	| **Set by**     | `AppBuilder::app_state()`     | Pre-dispatch hooks         |
512	| **Use for**    | Database, Config, API clients | User sessions, request IDs |
513	
514	### App State (Shared Resources)
515	
516	Configure long-lived resources at build time:
517	
518	```rust,ignore
519	App::builder()
520	    .app_state(Database::connect()?)
521	    .app_state(Config::load()?)
522	    .command("list", list_handler, template)?
523	    .build()?
524	```
525	
526	Access in handlers via `ctx.app_state`:
527	
528	```rust,ignore
529	fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
530	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
531	    let config = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Config>()?;
532	
533	    let items = db.query_items(config.max_results)?;
534	    Ok(Output::Render(items))
535	}
536	```
537	
538	### Extensions (Per-Request State)
539	
540	Pre-dispatch hooks inject request-scoped state:
541	
542	```rust,ignore
543	use standout_dispatch::{Hooks, HookError};
544	
545	struct UserScope { user_id: String, permissions: Vec<String> }
546	
547	let hooks = Hooks::new()
548	    .pre_dispatch(|matches, ctx| {
549	        // Can read app_state to set up per-request state
550	        let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
551	
552	        let user_id = matches.get_one::<String>("user").unwrap().clone();
553	        let permissions = db.get_permissions(&user_id)?;
554	
555	        ctx.extensions.insert(UserScope { user_id, permissions });
556	        Ok(())
557	    });
558	```
559	
560	Handlers retrieve from extensions:
561	
562	```rust,ignore
563	fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
564	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;       // shared
565	    let scope = ctx.extensions.get_required::<UserScope>()?;  // per-request
566	
567	    let items = db.list_for_user(&scope.user_id)?;
568	    Ok(Output::Render(items))
569	}
570	```
571	
572	### Extensions API
573	
574	Both `app_state` and `extensions` use the same `Extensions` type with these methods:
575	
576	| Method              | Description                                     |
577	| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
578	| `insert<T>(value)`  | Insert a value, returns previous if any         |
579	| `get<T>()`          | Get immutable reference, returns `Option<&T>`   |
580	| `get_required<T>()` | Get reference or return error if missing        |
581	| `get_mut<T>()`      | Get mutable reference, returns `Option<&mut T>` |
582	| `remove<T>()`       | Remove and return value                         |
583	| `contains<T>()`     | Check if type exists                            |
584	| `len()`             | Number of stored values                         |
585	| `is_empty()`        | True if no values stored                        |
586	| `clear()`           | Remove all values                               |
587	
588	Use `get_required` for mandatory dependencies (fails fast with clear error), `get` for optional ones.
589	
590	### When to Use Which
591	
592	**Use App State for:**
593	
594	- Database connections — expensive to create, should be pooled
595	- Configuration — loaded once at startup
596	- API clients — shared HTTP clients with connection pooling
597	
598	**Use Extensions for:**
599	
600	- User context — current user, session, permissions
601	- Request metadata — request ID, timing, correlation ID
602	- Transient state — data computed by one hook, used by handler
603	
604	### The Two-State Pattern
605	
606	The separation exists because:
607	
608	1. **Closure capture doesn't work with `#[derive(Dispatch)]`** — macro-generated dispatch calls handlers with a fixed signature
609	2. **App-level resources shouldn't be created per-request** — database pools and config are expensive
610	3. **Per-request state needs mutable injection** — hooks compute values at runtime
611	
612	```rust,ignore
613	// App state: configured once at build time
614	App::builder()
615	    .app_state(Database::connect()?)  // Shared via Arc
616	    .hooks("users.list", Hooks::new()
617	        .pre_dispatch(|matches, ctx| {
618	            // Extensions: computed per-request, can use app_state
619	            let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
620	            let user = authenticate(matches, db)?;
621	            ctx.extensions.insert(user);
622	            Ok(())
623	        }))?
624	```
625	
626	> For comprehensive coverage of state management patterns, see [App State and Extensions](app-state.md).
627	
628	---
629	
630	## Accessing CLI Arguments
631	
632	The `ArgMatches` parameter provides access to parsed arguments through clap's standard API:
633	
634	```rust,ignore
635	fn handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Data> {
636	    // Flags
637	    let verbose = matches.get_flag("verbose");
638	
639	    // Required options
640	    let name: &String = matches.get_one("name").unwrap();
641	
642	    // Optional values
643	    let limit: Option<&u32> = matches.get_one("limit");
644	
645	    // Multiple values
646	    let tags: Vec<&String> = matches.get_many("tags")
647	        .map(|v| v.collect())
648	        .unwrap_or_default();
649	
650	    Ok(Output::Render(Data { ... }))
651	}
652	```
653	
654	For subcommands, you work with the `ArgMatches` for your specific command level.
655	
656	---
657	
658	## Testing Handlers
659	
660	Because handlers have explicit inputs and outputs, their adapter behavior is
661	straightforward to test directly. Test validation, filtering, and state
662	transitions through the CLI-free library instead:
663	
664	```rust,ignore
665	#[test]
666	fn test_list_handler() {
667	    let cmd = Command::new("test")
668	        .arg(Arg::new("verbose").long("verbose").action(ArgAction::SetTrue));
669	    let matches = cmd.try_get_matches_from(["test", "--verbose"]).unwrap();
670	
671	    let ctx = CommandContext {
672	        command_path: vec!["list".into()],
673	        ..Default::default()
674	    };
675	
676	    let result = list_handler(&matches, &ctx);
677	
678	    assert!(result.is_ok());
679	    if let Ok(Output::Render(data)) = result {
680	        assert!(data.verbose);
681	    }
682	}
683	```
684	
685	No mocking frameworks needed—construct `ArgMatches` with clap, create a `CommandContext`, call your handler, assert on the result.
686	
687	### Testing with App State
688	
689	When handlers depend on app_state, inject test fixtures:
690	
691	```rust,ignore
692	#[test]
693	fn test_handler_with_app_state() {
694	    use std::sync::Arc;
695	
696	    // Create test fixtures
697	    let mock_db = MockDatabase::with_items(vec![
698	        Item { id: "1", name: "Test" }
699	    ]);
700	
701	    // Build app_state with test data
702	    let mut app_state = Extensions::new();
703	    app_state.insert(mock_db);
704	
705	    let ctx = CommandContext {
706	        command_path: vec!["list".into()],
707	        app_state: Arc::new(app_state),
708	        extensions: Extensions::new(),
709	    };
710	
711	    let cmd = Command::new("test");
712	    let matches = cmd.try_get_matches_from(["test"]).unwrap();
713	
714	    let result = list_handler(&matches, &ctx);
715	    assert!(result.is_ok());
716	}
717	```
718	
719	### Testing Handlers with Mutable State
720	
721	Handler tests can verify state mutation across calls:
722	
723	```rust,ignore
724	#[test]
725	fn test_handler_state_mutation() {
726	    struct Counter { count: u32 }
727	
728	    impl Handler for Counter {
729	        type Output = u32;
730	        fn handle(&mut self, _m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<u32> {
731	            self.count += 1;
732	            Ok(Output::Render(self.count))
733	        }
734	    }
735	
736	    let mut handler = Counter { count: 0 };
737	    let cmd = Command::new("test");
738	    let matches = cmd.try_get_matches_from(["test"]).unwrap();
739	    let ctx = CommandContext {
740	        command_path: vec!["count".into()],
741	        ..Default::default()
742	    };
743	
744	    // State accumulates across calls
745	    let _ = handler.handle(&matches, &ctx);
746	    let _ = handler.handle(&matches, &ctx);
747	    let result = handler.handle(&matches, &ctx);
748	
749	    assert!(matches!(result, Ok(Output::Render(3))));
750	}
751	```
752
